Union Warning Over Teachers Pay From Bbc Online

Sep 7, 2007 • Janice Cotcher

“Children’s education will suffer if teachers’ pay fails to keep pace with inflation, argues a teachers’ union.” (Last Updated: Sunday, 2 September 2007, 23:10 GMT 00:10 UK)

Let’s respond to some common complaints people give for raising teachers’ salaries before we look at its effects on quality of work:
Complaint: Teachers only work 10 months a year.
As a teacher, I work about 2000 hours a year or more. This includes the time I put in as yearbook adviser, coaching basketball, preparing lessons and marking. This is equivalent to someone who works 40 hours a week with only 2 weeks of vacation. I know some teachers put in the bare minimum of work and are not involved in extra-curricular activities but this is generally the exception to the rule. Once a teacher friend calculated she makes less than minimum wage for the number of hours a year she works.
Many schools make it a requirement that teachers be involved in a certain minimum number of activities. Some school boards offer non-monetary compensation for extra-curricular involvement. A previous employer offered an extra personal day for any teachers who logged more than 100 hours of more of extra-curricular supervision. As yearbook adviser, this was a pretty simple accomplishment. It was a nice gesture to show they appreciate the time I put in.
Reality: Teachers work just as much as you do — it is just condensed in a shorter amount of time.

Complaint: Teaching is easy; anyone can do it.
This is the response my former mentor gives to anyone to says that teachers have it easy. People tell him all the time how easy teachers have it — only work five hours a day, a week at Easter, two weeks at Christmas and all the major holidays and summer off. Encourages them to become teachers: “Come one, four years to the easy life!” They almost always respond, “I could never be a teacher”. It shuts them up pretty quickly.
Reality: You’re kidding me, right? What school did you go to? I’d love to teach there.Now the really question, will low teacher wages effect the quality of education? Absolutely, but that is just part of it. In order to remain a competitive employer, school boards need to increase wages to at least meet inflation. The field of education should attract the best and the brightest, wages and benefit are a start. People vote with their wallets. It isn’t that people don’t want teachers to get paid more; they don’t want to pay more taxes. Think how much professional athletes, actors, musicians get paid. Now, think how much you spend on entertainment in a week, month or year. Don’t convince yourself you can’t afford to pay more taxes when in reality you’d rather spend your money on other things.

People don’t realize that presently most teachers who are able to make a career in education have significant others who make a decent wage. I’m single and have a difficult time making ends met as a teacher. Trust me, I live very frugally. I scrimped and saved all year so I could afford to take the summer off. A lot of teachers I know work during the summer months (so much for the idea that teachers only work 10 months a year). During this past school year I took a job teaching night school two nights a week. Seemed like a good idea in theory. Suddenly I had an extra four hours a week that I had to prep for. I nearly had a nervous breakdown — it was not worth the money. If it wasn’t for my love of education (and frankly mathematics), I would not lasted this long in teaching.

There is a greater problem at hand than just wages: most school are horrible work environments and many teachers do not last more than 5 years. According to The Dimensions of a Great Place to Work® model, five components are needed: Credibility, Respect, Fairness, Pride and Camaraderie.

Credibility

“No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main.” - John Donne, Meditation XVII
Teachers should have pride in their work and rapport with other staff members. If we want students to have a quality education, the school must become a community. All staff and students must feel that they can be themselves, celebrate the successes of others and cooperate with others throughout the school. Teachers want to stay around for their careers.
